summary: This document provides a security framework for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). It covers the security aspects specific to MPLS-TP, which extends MPLS with new OAM capabilities, transport-style path protection, and heavy reliance on static provisioning. It describes potential threats and mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS-TP uses management messages and network paths that need protection. This RFC explains where trust boundaries lie, what can go wrong, and which defenses operators can consider.

subtitle: A threat model and defensive techniques for MPLS Transport Profile networks.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile adds in-band operations and maintenance messages and relies strongly on static provisioning, creating security concerns specific to these features.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines security reference models, describes threats to the data and management paths, and lists defensive techniques that operators can select for their environment.
tldr.outcome: This Informational framework supplements the general MPLS and GMPLS security framework in RFC 5920.

sections.title: What This Framework Covers
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) extends MPLS for packet transport networks. It adds operations, administration, and maintenance capabilities, transport-oriented path protection, and a strong emphasis on provisioning through network management systems.

This document focuses on security issues that arise from those MPLS-TP features. It builds on RFC 5920, whose general security models, threats, and defenses are assumed to apply as well.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP adds monitoring and protection functions to MPLS networks. This RFC focuses on the security issues created by those additions.

sections.title: Trusted and Untrusted Network Areas
sections.content:
A trusted zone is a part of the network under the complete operational control of one service provider. The location of service-provider boundaries determines which security model applies to a particular MPLS-TP network.

One model has a single provider control the path between its edge devices. Another covers networks where providers, customers, or partners control different parts of the path. In that case, a path may cross several trusted zones, and each boundary needs to be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted zone is the part of a network controlled by one provider. When several organizations control a path, the security review must include each boundary between them.

sections.title: Threats to Messages and Management
sections.content:
An attacker may insert, change, delete, or replay labels and operations messages carried over the Generic Associated Channel. Excessive in-band operations traffic can also consume bandwidth and cause congestion. These attacks could trigger an unwanted protection switch, prevent a path from being restored, or interrupt connectivity.

Management systems are another important target because they configure paths. An outside attacker, an insider with authorized access, or a compromised communication channel could cause false messages, path removal, incorrect endpoints, or denial of service. Operational errors can also create security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may forge or repeat network-monitoring messages, or send so many that they cause congestion. A compromised management system can also change paths or disrupt service.

sections.title: Defenses and Deployment Choices
sections.content:
The framework presents techniques rather than requirements for every deployment. It identifies authentication as a primary defense, including checking device and management-system identities, verifying message integrity, and detecting replay. Access controls, isolation, event logging, and defenses against denial of service are also relevant.

Dedicated infrastructure can reduce exposure. Operators can also verify connectivity along a path or between individual segments to detect accidental or deliberate misconnection. The provider should select techniques based on its service, trust boundaries, and operational environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can authenticate devices and messages, restrict access, isolate network resources, and record important events. The right combination depends on who controls each part of the network.
